passage:
Manager's note on annual reviews. Mohit, sales team.
This year I tried something different. Sudha is our star; her sales numbers are the best in the region, and in past years I simply rated her "outstanding" across the board. This time I rated each trait on its own and wrote an example for each before giving any score. Sales results: outstanding, clear numbers. Reliability: good, one missed client call. Communication with the team: I struggled to find an example, and two juniors said she rarely shares leads. So I rated it "needs work" and told her why, with the examples. She was surprised, then asked for ideas. It was a better conversation than any "outstanding" I've given before.

qa.q: What did two juniors say about Sudha?
qa.a: Two juniors said she rarely shares leads.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel about the "needs work" rating?
qa.a: She was surprised at first, likely because she was used to "outstanding" everywhere, then asked for ideas, showing she was open once the examples were clear.

qa.q: What did Mohit change in reviewing, and why is it fairer?
qa.a: Mohit rated each trait separately and wrote an example before any score, so her strong sales no longer lifted areas like team communication without evidence.

qa.q: How might the two juniors be affected by the new review?
qa.a: They may start getting more leads shared with them, since the gap they described was finally noticed and discussed.

grounding: Shows a fair reviewer rating each trait separately with examples so a star's strong sales do not lift every rating unearned.

passage:
Friday night
Review week. My first time rating my own team. Uday is everyone's favourite: funny, confident, the one clients ask for. My hand was about to tick "excellent" in every box before I had even read the form. I stopped. I made myself take the traits one at a time and write an example first. Client relationships: excellent, three renewals because of him. Documentation: I searched and found half his files incomplete. Deadlines: two late this quarter. In our meeting I asked him for his own examples. He laughed, then got serious and agreed about the files. It felt awkward, but honest. I'd rather be fair than liked.
Harsha

qa.q: How many renewals came because of Uday?
qa.a: Three renewals came because of Uday.

qa.q: Why was Harsha's hand about to tick excellent in every box?
qa.a: Uday is funny, confident and a client favourite, so that glow made every trait feel excellent before Harsha checked any evidence.

qa.q: What steps made Harsha's review fair?
qa.a: Taking each trait separately, writing an example before rating, and asking Uday for his own examples kept his strengths from covering the incomplete files and late deadlines.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after the review meeting?
qa.a: Uday may feel a little stung at first, but the specific examples let him accept the point about the files instead of feeling judged unfairly.

grounding: Shows a fair reviewer separating each trait and asking for examples so a popular colleague's charm does not lift every rating.

passage:
At the milk cooperative in a small town near Anand, Rashmi, twenty-four, was writing her first reviews for the collection team. Jeevan's name came first. He brought in the most milk every month, and the farmers along his route loved him. Her pen was already moving towards "excellent" in every column.
She stopped and split the page into three: reliability, record-keeping, working with farmers. Beside each she wrote, "Example?" Then she asked around.
The farmers told her Jeevan listened to every complaint and once came back at night when a cow fell ill. Excellent there. But the office clerk showed her the logbook: his entries were often filled in days late, from memory. Reliability was good; record-keeping needed work.
When she sat with Jeevan, she showed him the examples for each column. He nodded at the logbook one. "Fair," he said. "Nobody's ever told me that."

qa.q: How did Rashmi split the review page for Jeevan?
qa.a: She split the page into three: reliability, record-keeping and working with farmers.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel pulled to rate Jeevan 'excellent' in every column?
qa.a: He brought in the most milk and the farmers loved him, so his strong results made everything about him seem excellent before she had checked.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do before rating Jeevan, and why did it help?
qa.a: She wrote 'Example?' beside each trait and asked the farmers and the clerk, so each rating rested on its own evidence instead of his overall shine.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel hearing examples for each column?
qa.a: Jeevan seems to accept it because it is specific and fair, and perhaps a bit relieved that someone finally told him about the late logbook.

grounding: It shows a fair reviewer separating each trait and asking for examples before rating, so a strong performer is not lifted in everything unearned.

passage:
Omar ran the bike-repair workshop's small team in Kraków, and review week had come round again. Ivan was the obvious star: fastest mechanic, customers asked for him by name, and he made everyone laugh during the long winter shifts. Last year Omar had given him top marks everywhere without really thinking.
This year Omar printed the form with four separate lines: repair quality, speed, teamwork, paperwork. For each, he asked two colleagues for one real example, good or bad.
The examples surprised him. Repair quality and speed were outstanding. Teamwork was mixed: Ivan helped newcomers but sometimes took the best jobs for himself. Paperwork was weak; three warranty claims had been sent back for missing details.
When they met, Ivan was taken aback. "Paperwork? I thought I was your best guy."
"You are, at repairs," Omar said. "The rest I've scored on what people saw. Here are their examples."

qa.q: How many warranty claims had been sent back for missing details?
qa.a: Three warranty claims had been sent back for missing details.

qa.q: Why was Ivan taken aback by his review, and what does it show about his expectations?
qa.a: Ivan felt surprised and a little hurt, because being the obvious star with top marks last year made him expect a high rating on everything, including paperwork.

qa.q: What did Omar change in the process this year, and how did that help?
qa.a: He split the form into four lines and asked two colleagues for a real example for each, so outstanding repairs did not automatically lift teamwork and paperwork.

qa.q: How might the newer colleagues see the fairer review process?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that ratings rest on what people actually saw, not on who is funniest or fastest, which makes their own reviews feel fairer too.

grounding: It shows a fair reviewer rating each trait separately with real examples so that a star's strength in one area does not lift everything unearned.
